His other masterpiece, "The Old Regime and the Revolution," was published in 1856, three years before his death.
Gustave Flaubert was accused of seriously violating virtue, propriety, and religion in court for publishing his controversial novel "Madame Bovary." However, he was acquitted.

In 1894, a French spy discovered a handwritten memorandum at the German embassy containing confidential French military documents. Suspicion fell on Alfred Dreyfus, a Jewish captain, who was found guilty by a military court and sentenced to life imprisonment on Devil's Island. Dreyfus protested his innocence, but to no avail.
Let him rot on Devil's Island!

In 1896, Colonel Picquart discovered sufficient evidence suggesting that Major Esterhazy of the General Staff was the true author of the memorandum that had imprisoned Dreyfus, but the military court soon acquitted the major. In an open letter to the French President, Émile Zola accused the military court of the Major Esterhazy case of being obviously directed by the military. In late 1898, the evidence that had originally convicted Dreyfus was found to have been forged.

As evidence showed Dreyfus was innocent, his case was brought before the appellate court again in 1899. It was infuriating that he was found guilty again because the authorities refused to admit their previous mistake. Although he received a presidential pardon and was rehabilitated in 1906, the result of the affair increased anti-religious sentiment, anti-militarism, and united the French left.
Although Mount Pelée was considered dormant, it erupted catastrophically on May 7, 1902, killing over 30,000 people on the island of Martinique.

Fourteen-year-old Bernadette Soubirous first saw the Virgin Mary appear in a cave near Lourdes in the northern Pyrenees. In 1864 her testimony was recognized by the Church, and Lourdes quickly became a Catholic pilgrimage site.

The lady with the golden voice, Miss Sarah Bernhardt, will embark on a world tour with roles including Camille, Tosca, Phèdre, Adrienne Lecouvreur, and the role from "Hernani." Reportedly, this will be her last tour.
Louis Blériot became the first person to fly across the English Channel in his Type XI monoplane. He received a prize from the London Daily Mail.

Camille Jenatzky drove his automobile "La Jamais Contente" along the Route des Noyers near Saint-Germain to set the land speed record for a specific route, reaching a speed of 79.9 kilometers per hour.

Serge Diaghilev's ideas about ballet were not appreciated in his native Russia, so he moved to Paris, where he performed works by Stravinsky, Tchaikovsky, and Rimsky-Korsakov, and collaborated with famous ballet dancers such as Nijinsky and Balanchine.

Claude Monet was a painter who transitioned from Realism to Impressionism. In 1863 his work "Bath" (better known as "Luncheon on the Grass") caused a sensation in Paris due to its depiction of a nude woman.

To balance the budget, the Madrid government ordered the sale of church property. The Catholic Church's tax exemption was abolished, and instead the government agreed to bear the cost of maintaining churches.

General Narciso López, born in Venezuela, was executed by Spanish colonists in Cuba. After landing with a small group, he attempted to incite a rebellion to make Cuba join the United States, but ultimately failed due to lack of support.
To stop the destruction by Cuban rebels, the Governor ordered all citizens in the countryside to move to cities and live in tents, which would deny the rebels supplies and shelter.
We must restore order in Cuba!
We notice that many Cuban plantation owners want Cuba to join us. Perhaps Spain will sell the island?
Interested parties in North America have expressed interest in purchasing our Cuba.
No, Cuba will forever be the pearl of our Antilles
Well, Cuba can be taken, if the price is right
Should the King authorize a commission to discuss the urgently needed reforms in the Cuban colony?
Pablo Picasso, influenced by sculpture and African art, abandoned traditional painting methods in favor of a more conceptual style.

In 1855, Pascual Madoz, Minister of Public Wealth, ordered the expropriation of all public lands to address the government's fiscal deficit, which greatly strengthened the centralization of state power while fueling discontent among landless farmers.
We should find other ways to raise money.

After the Napoleonic-era guard was dissolved, the security of Spanish cities was entrusted to the National Militia, which was mainly composed of local militia. In 1844, the Marquis of Ahumada decided to create a national force directly under the Ministry of War. This force would be called the Civil Guard, replacing the unmanageable National Militia.
We are satisfied with the National Militia

In 1840, the Sultana arrived in New York, becoming the first Omani ship in history to sail to the New World. On board was a personal representative of Sultan Sayyid Said ibn Sultan, who would trade with the United States and meet with the U.S. government on behalf of the Sultan.
Under Sultan Said's rule, Zanzibar became the wealthiest province in the sultanate. When he died in 1856, the territories were divided into two parts for Majid of Zanzibar and Thuwaini of Muscat.
We cannot risk external forces interfering
Four years later, many in Zanzibar believed that given their greater wealth in Zanzibar, they no longer needed to be subject to Oman. Should we declare full independence from Oman?

Four years after Sultan Said's death, Majid refused to pay tribute to his brother Thuwaini. With British assistance mediated by Lord Canning, Governor-General of India, a deal was reached to pay tribute in exchange for recognition of Zanzibar's independence.

In 1885, Mark Twain published "Adventures of Huckleberry Finn," which completely changed American fiction. Before this book, traditional American novels used previous European linguistic forms, while Mark Twain used the speech of an American illiterate describing beautiful things to critique the original linguistic system. The book attempts to show that all kinds of people are respected for their actions rather than their status. At the time, the anti-traditional form caused such great controversy that its themes were overlooked. Even today people are a bit puzzled.
Well, then I'll go to hell too!
The Empire State Express, pulled by locomotive No. 999, set a record of 112 miles per hour on the New York Central and Hudson River Railroad.

Presidential candidate William Jennings Bryan called for unlimited silver coinage, which won him nominations from the Populist Party, Silver Republican Party, National Silver Party, and Progressive Party, uniting farmers from the West and South for the first time since the class struggle. His support for this policy was seen by northern industrialists as an attempt to obstruct creditors and destroy trusts.
You shall not press mankind upon a cross of gold

HMS Resolute was found floating in the North Atlantic. The ship had previously carried a squadron searching for the missing polar explorer Sir John Franklin, but later became trapped in ice and the crew had to abandon ship. The United States purchased the ship from its salvagers, restored it, and returned it to Britain.
It was right and proper to return it.
Statesman and lawyer Horace Mann began to reform the education system in Massachusetts. His school system eventually became a model for the entire United States.
The U.S. Congress established the Smithsonian Institution, which reports directly to the President. The institution is dedicated to scientific research, exploration, and popularization of science.
There are more things in heaven and earth...

Ralph Waldo Emerson's first volume of "Essays" was published in 1841, presenting a brand-new, quite mysterious native American philosophy to the world. Although many Europeans did not consider him a philosopher in his own right, his influence on European continental thought was immeasurable, especially in the case of Nietzsche.

In 1861, Oliver Wendell Holmes published "The Common Law," a historical book about the common law tradition. In the book he declared that law is not logical, and that judgments are better regulated by the specific circumstances of the time, or as one famous quote goes: "The life of the law has not been logic: it has been experience." After this book immediately became a classic, Holmes himself became a professor at Harvard the following year and eventually entered the federal Supreme Court. The publication of "The Common Law" marked the rise of pragmatism among American intellectuals and foreshadowed the distrust of moralism after the terrible bloodshed of the Civil War.
Law is what the sheriff obeys.
Personal Memoirs of Ulysses S. Grant

In 1885, Ulysses S. Grant published "Personal Memoirs," which almost completely recounted his life. He wrote this book while suffering from throat cancer to ensure his family would be well-provided for after his death. As a world-famous work in American English, Grant's memoir is unique in its simple, brisk style. Mark Twain considered it even better than Caesar's "Gallic Wars." "Personal Memoirs" was such a great success at the time that some copies were still being published after the Civil War. This is probably the best book ever written by a U.S. President.

Alfred T. Mahan published "The Influence of Sea Power Upon History," analyzing the importance of sea power to a nation through historical analysis. It was highly regarded by those who wanted to expand the navy and American territory.
Sea power is the guarantee of victory.

To address the growing anti-war sentiment and labor consciousness among conscripts and the lower classes, Congress passed amendments to the "Act of 1799 to Restrain Aliens from Opposing the United States and to Restrain Sedition" making it a crime in wartime to uphold the President and national policy and greatly harming the interests of foreign nationals and detainees. The Act was supported by the Supreme Court in subsequent decades and maintained in various forms until Justice Warren overturned it half a century later. During World War I, all 168 members of the executive committee of the Industrial Workers of the World were arrested on charges of attempting to undermine the federation.
When the state takes up the sword against her, that is treason
Dissent is the source of vitality for a free people

Private detectives have proven their efficiency in handling train robberies and capturing currency counterfeiters, and now they have become strikebreakers, also infiltrating secret societies such as the Molly Maguires.

Eight teams together formed a clean and well-managed baseball league: the Boston Red Caps, Chicago White Stockings, Cincinnati Red Stockings, Hartford Dark Blues, Louisville Grays, New York Mutuals, Philadelphia Athletics, and St. Louis Brown Stockings.
The fire started in the barn of Patrick O'Leary's house on DeKoven Street and spread to the business district, destroying 17,455 buildings, killing 300 people, and leaving 98,000 homeless.

A gunfight lasting about 30 seconds occurred in Tombstone, Arizona. Town Marshal Virgil Earp, Wyatt, Morgan, and Doc Holliday killed Billy Clanton, Tom McLaury, and Frank McLaury, all armed outlaws. The gunfight represented the coming of an era: American law would advance further into the remote frontier, further squeezing the living space of outlaws.
The first public baseball game was held in Cooperstown near New York. The New York Knickerbockers ultimately lost 1-23 to the New York Nine.
This will become a national pastime!

Francisco Madero issued a statement condemning fraud in the recent elections and declaring that Porfirio Díaz was no longer the legitimate President of Mexico. Madero called on citizens to take up arms against Díaz.
Francisco Madero was convinced that Pascual Orozco and Francisco Villa's uprising was intended to force Díaz from power.
Zapata's Peasant Army Joins the Revolution
Emiliano Zapata led a peasant uprising in the state of Morelos.
José Posada's satirical cartoons of the current regime landed him in prison again.
Through the 1860 agreement with the Vatican, relations with the Church were improved. Under the agreement, French clergy were allowed to return and church schools were established.
Faustin Soulouque, as the presidential candidate produced by a compromise between two factions in 1847, declared himself the second Emperor of Haiti: Faustin I.
José Batlle y Ordóñez, a famous journalist and leader of the Uruguayan Colorado Party, received strong support from the legislature for the political reforms he was implementing in Uruguay.
The time for reform has come.
In 1911, American explorer Hiram Bingham discovered the lost Inca city of Machu Picchu.
We have recovered part of our history!
Agricultural fertilizer made from guano has seen a surge in demand in Europe and North America. The rich guano deposits on our distant islands will become a major source of income for our country.
Smoking was increasingly becoming a widespread fashion. In 1837, Vienna authorities banned smoking in public places.

Emperor Francis I of Austria-Hungary died at the age of 67. His son succeeded him as Ferdinand I, who due to his large head and mental incapacity, was unable to handle state affairs, so a body called the Geheime Regierungskonferenz (Secret Government Conference) led by Clemens Wenzel von Metternich was formed to handle daily government affairs on his behalf.
To strengthen Hungary's position in the dual monarchy and national independence, Hungarian became the only language allowed to be spoken in the Hungarian parliament.
If it makes them feel better, let them speak Hungarian.
Serbian Ilija Garašanin called on South Slavs to unite and resist the Austrian and Ottoman oppressors in his work "Nastasye." His work became a guide for the Yugoslav nationalist movement.

Princess Elisabeth of Bavaria, known as "Sisi," married Emperor Franz Joseph I of Austria in 1854. Her often-commoner style, disregarding court formalities, won the love of the people. In 1898, she was assassinated in Geneva.

Since the talented Viennese designer Joseph Urban began his work at the Boston Opera House, the design of American theaters has clearly shifted to European style, becoming more vivid, more colorful, and giving audiences a more exciting experience.

The prefect of Schleswig proposes to reduce anti-German sentiments by enhancing German-language education and expelling the remaining Danish citizens from the province. Should we accept this proposal?
Schleswig is an indivisible part of Germany!
The Danes of Schleswig pose no threat to us
The Grand Theatre in Karlsruhe has been destroyed in a great fire. 63 people perished in the disaster.

The Valhalla near Donaustauf in Regensburg was opened to the public in 1842. It is a classical style memorial hall modeled after Greek temples, named after the legendary Norse underworld deity. In the hall of the memorial, there are busts of renowned Germans for public viewing.

The affair with dancer Laura de Montez proved to be the cause of King Ludwig's downfall (she was ennobled as countess by the latter). The conservative Catholic community strongly opposed their relationship, forcing the king to abdicate. Laura de Montez later died in poverty in New York.
The New Gallery, built in 1836, officially opened to the public in 1853. The collection focuses on the works of the Old Masters.

Composer Richard Wagner has finally completed the construction of the Bayreuth Festival Theatre. It is conceivable that the works of this great German composer will be performed at the annual Bayreuth Festival hereafter.
British Royal Family Separates from Saxe-Coburg-Gotha

Due to the recent war between Britain and Germany, our British cousins refuse to reclaim our honor! They now call themselves the House of Windsor, and now all families align with our duke, whose family will surely be treated harshly.
Blood is not thicker than water.

After extensive preparations, during the war with Schleswig-Holstein and Prussia, King Frederick VII of Denmark signed the constitution. The constitution allowed parliamentary elections and the submission of joint bills, ending the king's absolute rule. Although the king still had the power to appoint cabinet members from the majority party and approve legislation, this marked the first arrival of democracy in Denmark.
In 1871, Louis Pio founded the first Danish branch of the International, beginning to advocate for social reform and worker solidarity.

In 1872, after several months of strikes, Louis Pio convened a large open-air rally at Copenhagen Commons. Although the police allowed the rally to take place, large numbers of mounted police and military patrols clashed with striking workers. Fighting broke out, and the police arrested Louis Pio and a large number of socialist leaders. Pio was sentenced to five years in prison.
Louis Pio Forced to Leave the Country

In 1875, socialist leader Louis Pio was pardoned on the king's birthday and returned to lead the growing social democratic movement. However, his leadership style caused considerable discontent and conflict. In late 1875, he suddenly left for the United States. It was later learned that the police had paid him to leave.
Slave Rebellion in the Danish West Indies

In 1848, a slave rebellion broke out in the Danish Virgin Islands. Governor Peter von Scholten decided to quell the rebellion by emancipating the slaves rather than using armed force. Von Scholten invoked the 1847 law declaring all children born to slaves to be free. Von Scholten's actions faced fierce resistance from plantation owners. He was recalled to Denmark for trial, but the Supreme Court later acquitted him.
Between 1886 and 1892, over 25 modern fortifications were built on Zealand island to ensure that any threat from Germany would not succeed.
Von Koller Launches "Germanification" in Northern Schleswig

After losing the Slesvig region, Ernst Mathias von Koller conducted an oppressive Germanification campaign in the former Danish province. Danish residents were forced to use German as the only language of instruction in public schools, in accordance with laws issued earlier in 1888 that were now strictly enforced.
In 1899, a coalition of various trade unions formed a joint council and declared a general strike.

P.A. Alberti resigned as secretary to the Minister of Justice a month ago and surrendered. He was previously accused of embezzling over 15 million kroner from his own bank, equivalent to one-fifth of Denmark's annual budget. Alberti was found to have diverted treasury funds to pay off massive debts. His arrest led to the collapse of the government. Alberti and two accomplices who covered up his crimes have been indicted.
Selling the Danish Virgin Islands to the United States
After receiving a request from the United States to purchase the islands, a consultative referendum was held in 1917 on whether Denmark should sell the islands.
Agersnap published a novel in 1882 that proved to be helpful for the Danish minority in southern Denmark to maintain their Danish national identity.

The Danish Heath Development Company was founded in 1864 after the disastrous war and the loss of one-third of the country's territory. The company aimed to develop the heathlands of the Jutland peninsula, striving to "reclaim from within the land lost without."
Christiansborg Castle, rebuilt after a fire in 1794, caught fire again in 1884. The main part of the castle was destroyed and was not rebuilt until 1907 when the political atmosphere improved.

The New Carlsberg Sculpture Museum was founded in 1892 by Carl Jacobsen, owner of the New Carlsberg Brewery. Initially, the museum was mainly used to display Jacobsen's extensive collection of modern sculptures, and later ancient sculptures were also included.
Wonderful! Art belongs to the people!
Jakob Esprup, although serving as Prime Minister for many years, was not deeply popular. In 1885, a young socialist attempted to assassinate him, but the bullet hit a button on his coat.

Eleven breweries contributed to form a union in Copenhagen in 1891. It acquired the Tuborg brewery in 1894 and began cooperating with Carlsberg in 1903, gradually forming a strong brewing industry in Denmark. The Brewery Union and Carlsberg merged in 1969.

Jakob Christian Ellehammer was the first person in Denmark to build an aircraft. He made his first flight in December 1906. He had many other inventions, including refrigerators, hovercraft, and a helicopter that made its first flight on September 1, 1912.
In 1843, Danish writer and philosopher Kierkegaard published his work "Either/Or." Kierkegaard is generally considered to be the first existentialist philosopher.
Georg Carstensen opened the former Tivoli fortress in Copenhagen as the first true amusement park for entertainment and leisure.

This was the first time schools were established for the lower classes, especially farmers. Over the following decades, a considerable number of schools would be opened and greatly promote the development of education in rural areas. These schools accepted working girls and boys.

In 1871, Georg Brandes held the first lecture in a series of cultural lectures. He and his brother Eduard became central figures in Danish political and cultural debate, which culminated in the establishment of the "Policy" newspaper and a platform for liberal political thought.
Enhanced political awareness, the Liberal Party grew stronger

As American interests in the Caribbean region gradually increased, some advisors proposed purchasing the Danish West Indies, which would provide the United States with a strategic base to defend Caribbean sea lanes.
Historically, Denmark accepted the American proposal, but it is also possible that Denmark refused due to the low offer or the prevailing chauvinistic sentiment at the time.
Hendrik Conscience Publishes "The Lion of Flanders"

In 1838, Hendrik Conscience (1812-1883) published "The Lion of Flanders," his most popular Flemish novel of the 19th century and the first of his two masterpieces, the other being "The Battle of the Golden Spurs." "The Lion of Flanders" tells the story of the oppressed Flemish people's resistance against French rulers in the Battle of the Golden Spurs (1302). This novel was quickly adopted as the bible of the Flemish movement and remains a symbol of the Flemish people to this day.

1847 is considered the year of the Flemish movement's formation. This movement, which emerged from the convergence of voices from Belgian Flemish residents, broadly mobilized various Flemish organizations to participate, including sports clubs, music groups, theaters, intellectual organizations, etc. Initially, the movement was not political, but over the years, its followers increasingly tended toward violence under the sway of their firm beliefs. The Flemish movement would later lead to the formation of political parties seeking more rights for Flemish people in political life.
New ideas are being stirred up!

The years 1845 to 1850 were perhaps the worst period for Belgians, especially the Flemish people. The potato famine that began in 1845 led to the destruction of tens of thousands of infected potatoes. For rural Flemish people, this resulted in prolonged famine and poverty. This tragic period lasted until 1850.
We must lend a helping hand
Formation of the Free Trade Association

When the Belgian Free Trade Association was founded in 1846, Belgium was still suffering from the effects of the potato famine and the resulting famine. To ensure that the starving people had access to sufficient food, import duties on grain were abolished.

Adolphe Sax was a talented musician and instrument maker from Namur in southern Belgium. In 1846, he invented the remarkable instrument now known as the saxophone. This instrument was quickly accepted by Parisian musicians and later spread throughout the Atlantic world, used in various jazz band performances.
Solvay Invents the Industrial Alkali Process

Ernest Solvay (1838-1922) was one of the most gifted chemists in the world. One of the largest chemical companies in the world today, and the largest chemical company in Belgium, is named after him. In 1862, he invented the Solvay process for industrial alkali production. Industrial production using this method began in 1865.

In 1865, Father Damien de Veuster from Tienen in Brabant sailed to Molokai in Hawaii to help the lepers isolated there. He worked on Molokai and lived with the lepers for over 20 years. He died of leprosy in 1889.
In 1836, a group of liberals, following the example of the Tory Carlton Club founded in 1832, formed the Reform Club. Over the following decades, this club became the core of British liberalism.
Reform? Are you sure this is what we want!
In 1838, Charles Dickens' novel "Oliver Twist" was published in London. In this novel, he drew attention to the poverty and disenfranchisement of the working class at the time.

British painter and secular clergyman Thomas Cook organized the first backpacking trip, from Leicester to Loughborough. The low cost, including travel and accommodation, made it possible for more people to travel.
I can finally enjoy a vacation too!

On February 10, 1840, Queen Victoria married her cousin Prince Albert of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha. Unlike other marriages of the time, their union was based mainly on mutual affection rather than political alliance.
In June 1841, the first issue of "Punch" was published. This would become the longest-running, continuously published satirical magazine in history.
We'll keep an eye on them!
In 1844, George Williams founded the YMCA in London. This movement would spread worldwide and flourish for generations.
A fungus destroyed most of the potato harvest in Ireland in 1845. Famine followed.
I'm afraid we can do nothing!
In 1847, writer William Makepeace Thackeray published "Vanity Fair," a novel that satirizes the hollow and hypocritical so-called high society.
In 1850, the first telegraph line between Great Britain and the Continent was completed. This line crossed the English Channel connecting Dover and Calais, stretching 25 kilometers.

In 1851, the first Great Exhibition was held in London, with 13,937 exhibits from 15 countries astonishing 639,195 visitors. The Crystal Palace, built specifically for this exhibition, became a famous landmark.
George Bernard Shaw wrote an article entitled "The Essence of Realism" and organized the Independent Theatre Society to thoroughly introduce a new form of realism to the British stage.

William Butler Yeats' second collection of poems "The Rose" was published in 1893. His poetry uses unique diction and extraordinary rhythm, truly a work of genius. Yeats now developed a unique Irish theme and began a long association with Irish republicanism mixed with aesthetic mysticism.

Although he did not wish to be published during his lifetime, Gerard Manley Hopkins' poetry collection was published posthumously in 1918. His poetry introduced a new rhythm called "sprung rhythm" and gave new impetus to the growing modernist poetry movement. Hopkins' poetry, although modernist, is also considered religious poetry. He converted to Catholicism early in life and was a student and professor of medieval Christian philosophy.
After disaster comes harvest, and after the storm comes plenty?
Queen Victoria initiated the America's Cup competition for amateur sailors, held on the high seas. Since the 19th century, the trophy has been won by American teams every time.
Isambard Kingdom Brunel's steamship Great Britain became the first propeller-driven ship to cross the Atlantic Ocean.

At the ceremony marking 60 years of Queen Victoria's reign, the public celebrated with great affection. After a period of seclusion due to grief over her husband's death, Queen Victoria returned to the public eye through this ceremony.

The Corn Laws, originally designed to prevent large-scale foreign grain imports after the Napoleonic Wars, artificially kept food prices and farmers' profits high. In 1846, the Tory government led by Lord Robert Peel repealed the Corn Laws. This move marked the beginning of Britain's free trade policy that would last until the 20th century.
We cannot allow cheap foreign goods to flood our markets!
In 1857, the world's first climbing club was founded in London.

The first football club was founded in Sheffield and appropriately named FC Sheffield. The aim was to eliminate the confusion in rules after the popularity of rugby. The rules established by Sheffield became an integral part of the sport's development.

Florence Nightingale is universally recognized as the founder of modern nursing. During the Crimean War, the British Secretary of Defense appointed her as "Chief Nurse," leading 38 colleagues to a military hospital in Turkey. The resounding success of this mission led to the establishment of England's first nursing school and made people aware of the importance of urgently needed improvements in military medical services. Nightingale also made contributions to public health, medical administration, and health reform.

The first reform bill passed by Parliament still did not grant voting rights to the middle and lower classes, who launched a movement demanding broad democratization of Britain's constitutional system, and firmly advocated that the democratization of the country's economic and social life would improve the living standards of working people.
Reluctantly agree to some of their demands

In 1901, workers on the Taff Vale Railway in Wales struck back at the British House of Lords, which had previously ruled that trade unions should compensate employers for losses caused by strikes. This judgment dealt a heavy blow to trade unionists, while gaining much support for the nascent Labour Party.
The trade unions can count on the Labour Party

In 1882 at the Oval in London, England and Australia played the most memorable international cricket match in history. Over three days, the score fluctuated, and ultimately England lost by just seven runs in Australia's final innings. The match was played so intensely that one spectator died of a heart attack. The "Sporting Times" seized the opportunity to publish a famous obituary: "We deeply mourn the English cricket team, which died on August 29, 1882, to the heartbreak of thousands of grieving fans. May it rest in peace. The deceased's remains will be cremated and the ashes sent to Australia." Since then, the cricket series between England and Australia has been named the "Ashes."

Charles Darwin, based on observations from his famous voyage on the Beagle, synthesized the research of his contemporaries and wrote "On the Origin of Species." This book explained that the origin of all life on Earth stems from natural selection rather than divine creation. The fierce debate aroused by his views continues to this day.
Humans evolved from monkeys? You're kidding!

In 1877, the first men's singles lawn tennis championship held by the All-England Club and the British Lawn Tennis Association was held at Wimbledon in London, with Spencer Gore emerging as the champion. At the time, tickets cost one shilling per person, and about 200 spectators watched the final.
Jack the Ripper and London's Poverty

Jack the Ripper, reputed to be the most notorious serial killer of modern times, murdered at least six prostitutes, terrifying the Victorian authorities. Meanwhile, in the streets of London's East End, especially in the Whitechapel area plagued by murders, the shock and anxiety caused by these horrific murders indirectly aroused the British public's dissatisfaction with extreme poverty and the degradation of the ruling class. The authorities spent too much energy hunting for the madman who would never be caught, while the social problems caused by poverty would weigh heavily on the consciences of prosperous British people in the coming years.
Dedicated to catching the damned criminal!
Focus on solving the poverty problem!
Shakespearean Revival at Sadler's Wells Theatre

Samuel Phelps' production of Shakespeare's "A Midsummer Night's Dream" restored the original charm of the work. His simple style made this famous play a great success. Thereafter, almost every theater in England was determined to follow the trend he led. As a result, this revival brought many Shakespeare plays back to the stage.
Charles L. Dodgson published the first of his two children's books under the pen name "Lewis Carroll." Sir John Tenniel created the illustrations for this book.
The clipper ship Thermopylae set a record of 63 days on its maiden voyage from Gravesend to Melbourne.

Just 19 months after completion, the Tay Bridge across the Tay Estuary near Dundee was blown down by strong winds. A six-car train was lost. The bridge's designer, Lord Thomas Bouch, was held responsible for negligence and dismissed from his position as designer of the Forth Bridge.

Four clipper ships: the Blood Cross, Ariel, Taiping, and Serica, left Fuzhou at the end of May to compete in a race to bring back the first new tea of the year. The Taiping defeated her sister ships by half an hour, earning an extra 10 shillings per ton bonus.

Artist, entrepreneur, designer, and socialist William Morris broke Britain's reputation as a "poor country of decorative arts" by creating simple but beautiful furniture. His innovative slant-back ottoman chair became a classic.
Edward Elgar became a world-renowned composer through this piece. His large body of choral and orchestral works revived classical music in Great Britain.

As sports became increasingly popular, the first British Sports Festival was organized. Unlike the German gymnastics festivals, the sports festival focused on individual success rather than national celebration.
Are so many sports beneficial to health?

Partly due to the poor performance of the army in the Crimean War, and partly due to a clear tendency against the aristocracy, in 1871, the British Empire abolished the purchase of commissions. In the mid-1830s, a wave of religious fervor swept across America. Encouraged by preachers who called for a pious return to the original teachings of the Bible and a noble moral life, this movement gave rise to several new Protestant denominations that engaged in fierce theological and ritual debates with established churches, leading to schisms. This movement strengthened the power and influence of Christian teachings among the poor in America, at a time when religious fervor in Europe was declining.

In the early 19th century, a considerable number of Protestant denominations emerged in America, creating an environment for further theological reflection. The most influential movement among these was American Unitarianism. The emphasis on using reason to understand theology (thus rejecting the concept of the Trinity), the emphasis on the inherent divinity of humans, and the emphasis on human progress through reason gave Unitarianism great influence among the wealthy in the northwestern United States. At the same time, this movement encouraged some movements advocating social progress and the abolition of slavery through public education.
Faith and reason are reconciled for the betterment of humanity.

One direct impact of the religious awakening in early 19th-century America was the surge in the number of volunteer organizations organized to collectively address social and moral issues, helping the unfortunate and promoting their self-reliance through education. Historians call this the "Benevolent Empire." These organizations helped society build community infrastructure to promote rapid social expansion and change its appearance through new economic forces.

Hughes, who served as Bishop (later Archbishop) of New York from 1842 to 1864, worked tirelessly to promote the integration of Roman Catholics, especially newly arrived Catholic immigrants, into American society. At the same time, he had to maintain the institutions and assets of the Catholic Church, ensuring they remained firmly under the control of the Catholic hierarchy.

The religious awakening in American society in the early 19th century brought a series of impacts. Saloons were often their primary target, and sometimes fanatics would create violent incidents.

The independent Methodist church not only provided spiritual sustenance for African Americans but also provided a new platform to challenge the continued practice of slavery.

Louis Riel - The First Métis Rebel

Some French-Indian Métis in Manitoba had long hoped to gain autonomy. However, this dream was shattered when the Hudson's Bay Company territory was acquired by Canada. Under the leadership of Louis Riel, they rose up. Louis Riel was a man of firm faith who had studied to be a preacher in his early years. He fought for the Métis and became a local hero in Manitoba. After negotiations between Louis and the Canadian authorities, Manitoba gained a place in the federal government, and the Canadian representatives guaranteed that the rights of the Métis would not be violated. Thus, a small province - Manitoba - was born on the map of Canada.

Although the Canadian government promised to respect the rights of the Métis, their requests regarding their land and organizations were not taken seriously as promised. As immigrants from the east continued to invade their territories, the Métis gradually became disorganized. In early 1885, matters came to a head when the Métis rose up in rebellion again. Adopting a "Revolutionary Bill of Rights," the Métis established their own government and declared independence from Canada. Canadian troops arrived and suppressed the rebellion. Louis Riel was captured and executed. It was not until a hundred years later that the Métis became officially recognized citizens.

The resulting effects not only include the development of necessary equipment (e.g., landing craft specifically designed for amphibious operations), but also the creation and training of ground forces skilled in amphibious assaults, and the formulation of specific naval strategic tactics to optimize the deployment of warships in support and defense tasks during amphibious operations.

Naval exercises are an important element in naval warfare training. Ships can conduct simulated combat and other practical training tasks during exercises to understand how to respond during combat. Exercises can involve the entire fleet, and the duration varies from days to weeks. The importance of exercises is not only reflected in the training effects they bring, but also in evaluating the various abilities of officers and soldiers under pressure.

At the beginning of the 20th century, a large number of individuals entered the securities market, and buying on margin emerged as a way to increase the number of stocks with the lowest initial costs. The principle of buying on margin is: if the investment is profitable, the profits will cover the commission costs paid to purchase a large number of securities with the lowest initial costs. The risk of such investment is: if the investment incurs losses, the difference between the initial investment and the commission paid to purchase securities can only be borne by the investor. "What is the minimum margin requirement?" The securities industry has always been carefully debating this issue, because lower margins not only mean more investors with limited capital entering the market, but the associated risks may also make the investment unprofitable.

A functioning economy requires an effective monetary system, and smooth economic transactions require balanced monetary reserves. At the same time, a sound set of rules and regulations for this system is needed.

Refers to a monetary system based on silver. The government's cost of manufacturing currency is lower, which means the country will no longer experience currency shortages. However, there is a problem with the silver standard: the price of silver is dominated by the price of gold, so foreign trade becomes a trade that is "tasteless to eat, but too precious to discard."

By completely abolishing non-standard and unpopular monetary system classifications (e.g., guineas, shillings, etc.), a decimal monetary system is introduced, such as the system used by the United States (1 dollar equals 100 cents). This simplifies daily currency usage.

This refers to a system that uses both the gold standard and silver standard as parallel monetary units. This ensures that countries using this standard can always print currency at low costs, but the price difference between the two currencies will affect the lives of ordinary citizens.

This refers to a system for comparing the prices of different currencies, and also a simplified system for buying and selling currencies. It improves the efficiency of foreign trade, enabling it to develop by leaps and bounds.

Refers to a monetary system based on gold. The government's cost of printing currency is very expensive, and may sometimes lead to fewer currency reserves. However, the good news is: the price of gold is very stable, and at the same time, people's high trust in gold makes the currency more stable.

This refers to a system for comparing the prices of different currencies, and also a simplified system for buying and selling currencies. It improves the efficiency of foreign trade, enabling it to develop by leaps and bounds.
By establishing a sound state bond system, the government can issue bonds domestically and control monetary flow. This is an important way to achieve a stable monetary system.
By allowing the state bank to change interest rates, the government can at least partially balance inflation and reduce unemployment.

For many countries, the socio-economic pressures caused by other industrial countries investing in them during the war, and the resulting huge deficits, made it impossible for them to immediately return to the gold standard. In some countries, faced with new demands for revenue from new social responsibilities, often from newly participating countries or countries about to lose the war, these demands proved too large, and they planned to solve this problem by increasing the amount of currency in circulation. Without any policies or actions to guarantee the value of the currency, the result of this would be a rapid depreciation of the currency relative to other currencies or materials such as gold. Such government policies have harmful social impacts, affecting not only those living on limited or fixed incomes, but also those who have invested in rapidly depreciating currencies. For most countries, the state should make decisions about hyperinflation, and the market should respond simultaneously, jointly seeking alternative ideologies to restore social order and stability.

The scientific development of economics has had a tremendous impact on the functioning of the world economy at both the macro and micro levels. Merchants and nations alternately use various new ideas and knowledge to increase their efficiency.

John Elliot Cairnes was a follower of John Stuart Mill. His work "Slave Power" was a book defending the North in the American Civil War, which had a profound influence in England. In the book, he described non-competitive occupations in the labor market and was known for his distrust of mathematical economics. His most famous works are: "The Character and Logical Method of Political Economy" (1857) and "Some Leading Principles of Political Economy Newly Expounded" (1874).

Robert Torrens was a British army officer and the owner of the influential "Global" newspaper. Torrens independently applied Ricardo's "comparative advantage" to international trade (more precisely, he was an advocate of "reciprocal tariffs" rather than unilateral free trade). Torrens was also one of the discoverers of Ricardo's "differential rent" theory, although he later abandoned the Malthusian population theory that had been part of the theoretical foundation. Torrens was always critical of the "labor theory of value."

John Ramsay McCulloch was a prolific Scottish journalist and the most enthusiastic and dogmatic expositor of the classical Ricardian school. McCulloch began his career as editor of the "Scotsman" newspaper, then entered the Whig "Edinburgh Review" as economics editor until the late 1830s. McCulloch used his position at the "Review" to spread classical theory and promote his favorite economic policies (e.g., repealing the Corn Laws, retaining the Poor Laws, and legalizing trade unions). Between 1828 and 1832, McCulloch taught political economy at the University of London. In 1838, he became an auditor for the British Board of Works. McCulloch's major work "Principles" (1825) was possibly the first commercially successful economics "series" textbook (a work very faithful to Ricardian theory). However, in the development of economic theory, McCulloch is generally regarded as a "lightweight" figure. His main contribution was the short-lived "wages fund" theory (1824, 1825, 1826). McCulloch was also the editor of the 1828 edition of Adam Smith's "Wealth of Nations" and the 1846 edition of David Ricardo's works. He also produced some of the earliest accounting theories related to economic thought (of course, also focused on Ricardian theory). His commemorative 1837 agreement shows statistical accounting errors in Malthusian population theory.

This economist's works have been printed in various languages and widely circulated. While academies were still debating and refining their respective opinions, its merits were quickly understood by the general public. At this point, it changed the economic behavior and processes of nations.

James Mill was a radical thinker who worked under the shadow of Jeremy Bentham. These two men were known as the founders of utilitarianism, and their main practical applications were explained in detail in Mill's works: "Elements of Political Economy" (1821) and "Analysis of the Phenomena of the Human Mind" (1829).

John Stuart Mill was the son of the famous utilitarian James Mill, and he quickly became one of the focal points in all of Britain with his intelligent mind and more radical attitudes. He published several books, including "A System of Logic" (1843), "Principles of Political Economy" (1848), "On Liberty" (1859), and "Considerations on Representative Government" (1861), which made him a central figure in social liberalism and social thought.

Proudhon was apprenticed to a printer, and became interested in politics when he began printing Charles Fourier's "Emerging Industry and the Cooperative World." Subsequently, Proudhon began writing and published "What is Property?" in 1843. In the book, Proudhon attacked the unjust nature of inequality and coined the phrase "Property is theft." In 1846, Proudhon published his most important work: "System of Economic Contradictions." Karl Marx wrote "The Poverty of Philosophy" (1847) in response to Proudhon's book. Thus, the two men began a long intellectual confrontation. Proudhon opposed Marx's authoritarianism, and his main influence was in the libertarian socialist movement.

Karl Marx was a true disciple of Hegel, but he developed his own idealist philosophy. Later, he first began to associate with the working class in Paris. Marx was deeply shocked by their poverty, but impressed by their camaraderie. In an article he wrote for the "German-French Annual," Marx applied Hegel's dialectical development theory to what he saw in Paris. From then on, Marx declared himself a communist, advocating that the working class (proletariat) would ultimately become the liberators of society. Marx's most influential works include: "The German Ideology," "The Communist Manifesto," "Principles of Communism," and "Das Kapital." He lived most of his life in England, where he published his works and became the most influential socialist in history.

Engels went to Manchester as a young man to help his father manage a cotton factory. Engels was deeply shocked by the poverty in the city and wrote an article, published as "The Condition of the Working Class in England" (1844). Engels met Marx here, and thereafter devoted his entire life to writing and trying to establish international workers' organizations with Marx. Engels wisely chose to live under Marx's shadow, but he financially supported Marx to facilitate his writing. Fundamentally, without Engels, there would be no Marx
column3: and vice versa.

column2: Eduard Bernstein was originally a staunch believer in Marxism and began his political career in the German Social Democratic Party, but during his subsequent years in London, Bernstein gradually discovered that the best way to achieve socialism in an industrialized country was through trade union activities and parliamentary politics. He published a series of articles arguing that Karl Marx's predictions about capitalist development would not be realized. He pointed out that workers' real wages had been growing, and that the class polarization between the oppressed proletariat and the capitalists had not materialized. Capital was not held only by a few people. Bernstein's revisionist views appeared in his most influential work "Evolutionary Socialism" (1899).

Webb developed socialist ideas while at university, and joined the Fabian Society in 1885. The society believed that capitalism created an unfair and inefficient society. Members agreed that the group's ultimate goal should be to "reconstruct society according to the highest moral standards." The Fabian Society was an organization that "sought and exposed facts," and it printed a series of pamphlets covering various social issues. Most of these pamphlets were written by Sidney Webb, including "Socialism in England" (1887), "The London Programme" (1888), and "Eight Hours Day" (1891). Webb co-wrote "The Labour Party's Election Manifesto" with George Bernard Shaw. Later, Webb became an important figure in social democracy and had some influence in international workers' organizations.

Karl Kautsky joined the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and drafted the Erfurt Program, which declared that the SDP was the evolutionary Marxist organization. He also wrote "Karl Marx's Economic Doctrines" (1887) and "Thomas More and His Utopia" (1888). He initially believed Bernstein's theory was correct, but later broke with Bernstein and continued to uphold his more reformist views on socialism.

In 1885, Jaurès was elected as a deputy to the Chamber of Deputies. After losing the 1889 election, he returned to the University of Toulouse. His political views became increasingly radical, and after reading Marx's works, he began to advocate socialism. He was not a revolutionary and supported independent socialists. While serving as a deputy, Jaurès completed his massive work "History of the French Revolution in the Socialist Perspective." In 1904, he also co-founded the left-wing newspaper "L'Humanité" with Aristide Briand and René Viviani. At the beginning of the 20th century, a new socialist party led by Jaurès developed rapidly, but there were divisions over the correct response to German militarism. Jaurès advocated an international arbitration policy, while others supported the Triple Entente.

Friedrich List was a nationalist, a moderate critic of economic theory, and one of the founders of the German historical school. His best-known work "The National System of Political Economy" (1841) was originally written to oppose the free trade doctrines of classical economics. However, he was not a supporter of trade protectionism. Based on his own analysis of economics, he advocated adding political factors (particularly "national" political factors) to economics. List argued that the government's responsibility was to promote the nation's "productive forces," and when productive forces were in place, to begin free trade, but never prematurely. This is similar to the modern debate over whether to protect "infant industries." In addition, he developed a theory of economic "stages," which served as the blueprint for the German historical school.

Professor at the University of Leipzig (1848-1894), he was the founder of the German historical school of economics and opposed the classical laissez-faire policy view. Roscher's works emphasized the developmental characteristics of capitalism through detailed analysis of the culture of ancient countries in history. His "System of Political Economy" (1878 edition of "Principles of Political Economy," translated 13th edition, 1854-94, 5 volumes) was one of the most influential textbooks in the second half of the 19th century. His most famous work is "History of German National Economy" (1874).

Hildebrand was a sharp critic of classical theory, and spent a lot of time mercilessly attacking Ricardo's materialism, universalism, and cosmopolitanism. In his later years, he wrote down his thoughts, actually developing a linear "step" theory of economic history. But his empirical and statistical works did not use these profound insights.

Knies's linear step theory involved "moral progress," but this alone could consign most theories to the garbage heap of history. However, his 1873 work included a small part of historical method. His involvement in politics resulted in a brief period of exile in 1848. He wrote: "Political Economy from the Standpoint of Historical Method" (1853) and "Money and Credit" (1873).

Schmoller opposed neoclassical economics and engaged in a famous methodological debate with Carl Menger (the "Methodenstreit"). Although many said he lost the debate by refusing to participate (reportedly, after receiving Menger's invitation, he returned it unread and published a "half-review" claiming "the letter is not worth reading at all"), Schmoller retained his administrative power over the German university appointment system and excluded classical and neoclassical economic theory from the German teaching system, which made him famous
column3: the only one capable of rivaling him was Menger's Austrian school. Gustav Schmoller's involvement in politics was also particularly important: in 1872, he founded the Social Policy Association, an organization of conservative economists supporting the corporatist "state-industry-labor axis" theory. Liberals strongly condemned their advocacy of state interventionism and labeled Schmoller and the historical relativists "socialists of the chair" - mocking them for never deigning to ask questions.

column2: Although Wagner was a more active member of Schmoller's association, he supported Menger in the Methodenstreit. He devoted himself to the study of public finance, which was his strongest subject in economics. Outside economics, he was a friend of Lassalle and Rodbertus - although he did not fully share their socialist ideals, and with his stronger conservative nature in political affairs, Wagner offered severe criticism of unbridled capitalism and suggested that the state should alleviate the burdens on the labor force. He wrote "Science of Finance" Volumes 1-4 (1877-1901) and "Foundations of Political Economy" (1876).

Cunningham was an outspoken opponent of the emerging neoclassical economics, a title actually given to him by his colleague Alfred Marshall and Cambridge College. In economics, he sought to promote historical theory, making him one of the most important advocates of the British historical school. Despite being attacked, Marshall was swayed by his constant entreaties and decided to try to include more historical content in his works and make his economic principles more "inductive." However, he refused to accept Cunningham's main idea - that the validity of economic laws should be combined with historical, social, and cultural contexts. Cunningham not only opposed the methodological approach in neoclassical economics but also pointed fingers at politics. Cunningham strongly opposed utilitarian philosophy and laissez-faire policies, and wrote several pamphlets defending trade unions and trade protectionism. He also had great interest in old mercantilist ideas.

Johann Heinrich von Thünen was a North German landowner from Mecklenburg. Although educated at Göttingen, he spent most of his life managing his rural estate, Tellow. In his first volume of "The Isolated State" (1826), he combined rent theory with the first serious discussion of spatial economics. His second volume (1850) developed the essence of marginal productivity distribution theory with precise mathematical methods, making him one of the most important original marginalists of the era. Before his death, he asked that his famous equation for the marginal product of labor or the natural wage be engraved on his tombstone.

French economist Léon Walras was praised by Joseph Schumpeter as "the greatest of all economists." Walras was one of the three leaders of the marginal revolution, although his greatest work "Elements of Pure Economics" was published in 1874, three years later than the works of William Stanley Jevons and Carl Menger. Nevertheless, among the three revolutionaries, Léon Walras presented the new "marginalism" or "neoclassical" theory in a formal general equilibrium setting. Thus, he gave marginal theory the multi-market considerations that Jevons largely avoided and the mathematical precision that Menger avoided. Léon Walras is widely and reasonably regarded as the father of general equilibrium theory.

Jevons's influence on economics was enormous. As the father of neoclassical economics, his legacy has been greatly admired and well preserved. However, for some reason he did not achieve his expected goals. Jevons could have achieved more ambitious goals, integrating his profound insights into simple exchange into a broader range of theories in a more systematic and persistent way, such as production, capital, money, and business cycles, which would have consigned the Ricardian school to the history of economics. If Jevons had not died young, he might have completed the aforementioned vision, but a subsequent economics paper he wrote (published posthumously in 1905) did not seem intended to achieve this ambitious goal. Moreover, at the time of his death, the marginalist revolution was still in its initial stages. It was still experimental, not yet a stable and complete system, merely a scientific hypothesis that could not yet become an independent discipline. It is worth noting that Jevons also added considerable philosophical ideas to economics, which was one of his achievements.

Carl Menger was praised by William Stanley Jevons and Léon Walras as one of the three leaders of the marginalist revolution in the 1870s. However, Menger's "Principles," published in 1871, avoided all the mathematical foundations described by the other two revolutionaries. Therefore, many economists believed Menger should not be called a revolutionary. In a sense, he was not the "revolutionary" people imagined. Carl Menger was different from Jevons or Walras
column3: he established a proper "school of thought," the so-called school that more or less retains its unique characteristics - the "Austrian School" reflects this from its name. He had two disciples in Vienna, Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser, who did a great deal for the development and advancement of the school.

column2: Thorstein Veblen's importance to economics is like Jonathan Swift's importance to English literature: a master of satire. The essence of satire is that its message must be ambiguous: the reader cannot be sure whether the author is narrating very seriously or just joking. Such qualities appear in Swift's "Gulliver's Travels," and similar characteristics are reflected in Veblen's theories. His works include: "The Theory of the Leisure Class" (1899), "The Instinct of Workmanship" (1914), "Imperial Germany and the Industrial Revolution" (1915), "The Higher Learning in America" (1918), "Absentee Ownership" (1923), and many short essays. In fact, with the exception of "The Theory of Business Enterprise" (1904), the articles and books he wrote contain such characteristics, and his books or articles show almost no trace of academic works. Opening any of his books, we find this idea: modern industrial society is the product of extreme contradictions, the contradiction between "pecuniary employment" and "industrial employment," between "business enterprise" and "mechanical craftsmanship," between "market value" and "serviceability," in short, between making money and producing. There is a class that struggles constantly under capitalism, but not the middle class and the proletariat, but the struggle between merchants and engineers. Intellectual habits unite bankers, brokers, lawyers, and managers into a defense line protecting private property.
He was the first, and the most important, the wisest, and the purest theorist.

French philosopher, mathematician, and economist Augustin Cournot was hailed as one of the greatest marginalists. His major economic work "Researches into the Mathematical Principles of the Theory of Wealth" (1838) involved very unique views, which no one could match. Although he was not valued in his own time, Cournot's works are invaluable to modern economics.

Jules Dupuit was probably the most eminent French engineer-economist. After training at the École Polytechnique in Paris, Dupuit began his brilliant career as a civil engineer. Inspired by infrastructure construction, he decided to go deeper into economic theory.

Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto was one of the leaders of the Lausanne school and an outstanding member of the "second generation" of the neoclassical revolution. Although his influence was limited during his lifetime, his "trial and error" approach to general equilibrium theory was reused in the "Pareto revival" of the 1930s, and has since become a guiding method for many economists.

Knut Wicksell was a Swedish economist. He pioneered the use of the term "natural rate of interest" to describe the interest rate in a state of long-run economic equilibrium. Wicksell had a major influence on later Nobel laureate economist James M. Buchanan. According to Buchanan, his own public choice theory "was almost a necessary product after I absorbed the essence of the Wicksellian school." Public choice theory holds that economists should no longer treat the government as a benevolent dictator. Wicksell was a disciple of Malthus and strongly advocated birth control. He often spoke on moral issues. His most famous work is "Interest and Prices," which presented the Wicksellian version of the quantity theory of money. Unlike the mainstream view of the time, he saw that the money supply could indirectly affect prices. Wicksell also refined the theory of marginal productivity, pointing out that the remuneration for factors of production should equal their marginal productivity. He also pointed out that the most efficient allocation of resources is not necessarily the most fair allocation of resources, because before resource allocation takes place, there already exists an income distribution pattern that may not be fair. The efficient allocation of resources depends on this pre-existing income distribution pattern. The later Swedish Stockholm school developed its own unique set of macroeconomics based on Wicksell's "theory of quantity and price."

Irving Fisher was one of the earliest American neoclassical economists with exceptional mathematical talent. In the "marginal theory revolution" of neoclassical economics, Fisher made many significant contributions. This Yale economist was an eccentric and colorful figure. In 1892, while writing his doctoral thesis, he built a complex machine with pumps, wheels, levers, and tubes to illustrate his price theory. Here are his drafts and the first two machine prototypes. He was also an active advocate of eugenics and healthy eating. His visible card holder - now called a "rolodex" - made him a fortune. He advocated a banking system requiring 100% full reserve requirements. In the 1929 Wall Street crash, his wealth and reputation plummeted. Because just days before the crash, he had assured investors that stock prices were not artificially inflated, but had genuinely risen to a new price plateau.

After receiving his doctorate in Vienna, Schumpeter did not return to academia but worked as a freelance lawyer for several years until 1909. While teaching in Czernowitz (now in Ukraine), he wrote "The Theory of Economic Development" (1911), in which he first expounded his famous concept of "entrepreneurship." He believed that innovative entrepreneurship, even under fierce competition and declining profits, could bring technological and financial innovations. And it was this spirit that provided the driving force for economic growth. In 1919, Schumpeter became Austria's Minister of Finance, unfortunately catching up with the period's hyperinflation, and was dismissed from office that year. Although his forte was teaching, Schumpeter completed three new works at Harvard, including "Business Cycles" (1939) and the famous "Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy" (1942). In that book, Schumpeter made his famous prediction: capitalism would head toward destruction under the leadership of elite-controlled governments.

Böhm-Bawerk's scholarly career was intermittent. The most important academic activity spanned his years at the University of Innsbruck (1881-1889). It was in the 1880s that he first published two of the three volumes of his magnum opus "Capital and Interest." His main work in later years was serving as Austrian Minister of Finance, a position he held throughout the 1890s and beyond, although not continuously
column3: his portrait appeared on the Austrian 100-shilling note, which gave him some respectability. After holding this position and other government duties, he returned to teaching in 1904. After becoming chairman at the University of Vienna, he was a colleague of Wieser, who was the successor to his colleague Menger. In the last ten years of Böhm-Bawerk's career (he died in 1914), the students he taught included Joseph Schumpeter and Ludwig von Mises.

column2: British economist, one of the most influential economists of modern Western economics. The macroeconomics he founded, together with Freud's psychoanalysis and Einstein's theory of relativity, are known as the three revolutions in human knowledge in the 20th century. Keynes believed that in real life there are three psychological laws: diminishing marginal propensity to consume, diminishing marginal efficiency of capital, and liquidity preference. Due to the existence of these laws, with the development of society, there will inevitably be a problem of insufficient effective demand. Insufficient effective demand makes enterprises unable to sell what they produce, leading to factory shutdowns and even bankruptcies, ultimately causing the outbreak of capitalist economic crises and workers' unemployment. He believed that severe unemployment was caused by insufficient consumer demand and could be alleviated through some government-funded projects. He also advocated government stimulating economic activity through deficit spending.
British economist, student of Keynes, who first proposed the theory of the consumption multiplier effect.

Austrian economist, radical laissez-faire advocate, major influence on the modern libertarian movement, and a scholar who promoted the revival of classical liberalism. He was hailed as the "dean of the Austrian School of Economics" and called the libertarian century figure. His theories also influenced later economists such as Friedrich Hayek and Murray Rothbard, among whom his student Hayek won the Nobel Prize in Economics on behalf of liberalism in 1974.

Hayek was a British economist and political philosopher born in Austria. He was known for his insistence on free-market capitalism and opposition to socialism, Keynesianism, and collectivism. He is widely regarded as one of the most important members of the Austrian School of Economics, and he also made considerable contributions to the fields of jurisprudence and cognitive science. In 1974, Hayek won the Nobel Prize in Economics together with his theoretical opponent Gunnar Myrdal, "in recognition of his pioneering research on monetary policy and business cycles, and his penetrating analysis of the interactive influence of economic, social, and institutional factors." In 1991, Hayek was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by the President of the United States in recognition of his "lifelong vision."

With the development of the 20th century, new economic development models adopted by certain societies flourished outside the capitalist world, and some politicians began to think about the feasibility of combining the advantages of capitalist economy and planned economy for the benefit of society as a whole. The result is that some governments, while ensuring the basic capitalist elements within the fundamental economic structure, introduce government-guided elements in specific economic fields. Although many ideologically-driven critics either think the policy has gone too far or that the economic transformation is insufficient, given the remarkable effectiveness of mixed economies in restoring economic production and alleviating social contradictions, they still leave a deep impression.

The state plans in advance in all aspects of production, resource allocation, and product consumption. Since almost all planned economic systems rely on government directive plans, they are also called "command economies," thus avoiding the blindness and uncertainty of market economic development and the harm caused to social and economic development. Such as: duplicate construction, vicious competition among enterprises, factory closures, workers' unemployment, unbalanced regional economic development, and the emergence of social and economic crises.
A policy of self-sufficiency in which a country does not rely on imports or economic assistance.

A country adopts various measures to restrict the import of certain foreign industrial products, promote the production of related domestic industrial products, and gradually replace imported goods with domestic products in the domestic market, creating favorable conditions for the development of domestic industry and achieving industrialization. The general approach is that the state encourages foreign private capital to establish joint ventures or cooperative enterprises in the country by granting preferential treatments in taxation, investment, and sales
column3: or improves the level of industrialization through processing trade methods such as incoming material and incoming components processing. To enable domestic substitute industries to develop, methods such as raising tariffs, implementing quantitative restrictions, and foreign exchange controls must be used to restrict the import of foreign industrial products, so that domestic industries competing with imports can grow and develop under conditions of little or no competition.
